one_line_idea: Test-time adaptation hyperparameters are implicitly tuned on the test distribution, making reported gains circular; shift-blind hyperparameter selection erases most of them.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Test-time adaptation has no labeled validation data by definition, yet published methods report specific learning rates, momentum values, and update schedules that vary per benchmark.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The published hyperparameters encode oracle knowledge of the test shift, and under a rigorous protocol where hyperparameters must be fixed before seeing the shift, most methods lose most of their advantage over the unadapted baseline.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Selecting each method's hyperparameters on one shift family and deploying them unchanged on a different shift family will reduce average gains substantially and cause negative gains for some method-shift pairs. Falsified if: under shift-blind hyperparameter transfer (hyperparameters selected on one shift family, deployed unchanged on a different family), zero (0) method-shift pairs show negative adaptation gain (gain < 0 relative to the unadapted baseline), i.e. every tested method-shift pair keeps a non-negative gain.
why_important: If gains require knowing the shift in advance, the methods do not solve the stated problem, since knowing the shift in advance would allow far stronger interventions.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Oracle model selection has been criticized in domain generalization, but an equivalent formal audit for the test-time adaptation literature, with cross-shift hyperparameter transfer as the headline protocol, may not exist.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Define a shift-blind protocol where hyperparameters are chosen on held-out synthetic shifts only, then evaluate several published methods on disjoint shift families and compare to their published-configuration results.
main_risk: Some gains may be genuinely hyperparameter-insensitive, so the audit must report per-method sensitivity rather than a single aggregate to avoid overclaiming.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Readers generally assume reported test-time adaptation gains would survive honest hyperparameter selection because the methods are described as unsupervised.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Unsupervised objectives like entropy are known to be unstable to learning-rate choice, and instability plus per-benchmark tuning is the classic signature of oracle selection.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Take two published methods, swap their per-benchmark hyperparameters across benchmarks, and check whether gains survive the swap on one backbone in a day.

one_line_idea: A frozen foundation model with a test-time nearest-neighbor or retrieval-augmented classifier matches gradient-based test-time adaptation at far lower risk.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Gradient-based test-time adaptation mutates model parameters on unlabeled data, which introduces collapse and drift risk, while nonparametric classifiers over frozen features can also absorb test-distribution information without touching weights.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Accumulating test embeddings in a memory and classifying by neighborhood vote or prototype update captures most of the benefit that parameter-updating adaptation achieves, because the useful adaptation signal is a shift in feature-space class geometry rather than in the features themselves.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On standard adaptation benchmarks with a strong frozen backbone, a memory-based nonparametric adapter will reach a large fraction of the gain of gradient-based methods while never degrading below the zero-shot baseline on any tested shift. Falsified if: the memory-based nonparametric adapter degrades below the zero-shot baseline (per-shift accuracy gain < 0 percentage points) on one or more tested shifts.
why_important: If true, deployments get most of the robustness benefit with a mechanism that is trivially reversible, auditable, and immune to weight collapse.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Prototype and memory ideas exist in the literature, but a head-to-head risk-versus-gain comparison framing nonparametric adaptation as a safety-dominant substitute for gradient adaptation on foundation models may be unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement a streaming prototype or nearest-neighbor head over a frozen public backbone, compare against two gradient-based methods on the same shifts, and report both average gain and worst-case degradation.
main_risk: Memory-based methods depend on class balance in the stream, and heavily skewed streams could poison prototypes in a way that mirrors gradient collapse.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The field treats parameter updating as the substantive form of adaptation and nonparametric heads as weak baselines.
why_it_might_be_wrong: With strong pretrained features, most shift-induced error is arguably in the classifier geometry, which is exactly the part a nonparametric head can fix without gradients.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One backbone, one shift suite, streaming prototype head versus one entropy-minimization method, compare gain and worst-case drop in an afternoon.

one_line_idea: Most of what test-time adaptation improves is calibration and decision thresholds, not representation quality, and a post-hoc output correction recovers the bulk of its accuracy gain.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Test-time adaptation methods update internal parameters and report accuracy improvements under shift, but the mechanism of improvement is rarely decomposed.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The dominant effect of popular adaptation methods is equivalent to a shift-conditional rescaling and re-prioring of the output distribution, so a purely post-hoc correction that estimates test-class marginals and temperature achieves most of the same accuracy gain without touching features.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across several methods and shifts, an output-layer-only correction pipeline will recover a majority of the accuracy gain of full adaptation, and the residual gain attributable to feature change will be small and shift-dependent. Falsified if: the output-layer-only correction pipeline (label-marginal + temperature fit on the same unlabeled test data) recovers <= 50% of the full-adaptation accuracy gain across the tested methods and shifts.
why_important: If gains live in the output layer, the field can replace risky weight surgery with cheap, transparent probability corrections and redirect research toward the genuinely hard residual.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Mechanistic decompositions of where adaptation gains come from, separating output recalibration from representation change with matched-budget baselines, appear rare.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For each method and shift, fit a label-marginal and temperature correction on the same unlabeled test data the method uses, compare accuracy gains, and measure feature-space movement to correlate residual gains with representation change.
main_risk: Estimating test-class marginals without labels is itself error-prone, and a weak estimator could understate how much of the gain is output-level.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Adaptation is assumed to repair internal representations damaged by shift, which is why parameter updates are considered necessary.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Entropy-style objectives act most directly on logit sharpness and class priors, so the output-level interpretation matches the objective's actual gradient structure.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One method, three shifts, compare entropy-minimization gain to an unlabeled temperature-plus-prior correction on the same test batches in a day.

one_line_idea: Periodic hard reset to source weights beats sophisticated anti-forgetting machinery in continual test-time adaptation over long horizons.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Continual test-time adaptation methods add mechanisms like stochastic weight restoration and regularization toward source to prevent drift, adding complexity and hyperparameters.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The entire benefit of these mechanisms is approximated by periodically resetting all adapted parameters to the source checkpoint, because the useful adaptation state is cheap to reacquire while accumulated drift is expensive to undo.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On long non-stationary streams, plain adaptation plus periodic reset will match or exceed dedicated continual-adaptation methods across most shift sequences, for some reset period spanning a wide tolerant range. Falsified if: plain adaptation plus periodic reset (at its best tested reset period) matches or exceeds the dedicated continual-adaptation methods' time-averaged accuracy on <= 50% of the tested shift sequences.
why_important: If a one-line baseline matches complex methods, the field's complexity is unjustified and evaluation practice failed to include the obvious control.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Reset appears as an ablation in some papers, but reset-period sweeps positioned as the primary baseline for the continual adaptation literature seem absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run two dedicated continual-adaptation methods and reset-augmented plain adaptation on standard corruption sequences and one natural drift stream, sweeping reset period logarithmically, and compare final and time-averaged accuracy.
main_risk: Reset timing may interact badly with abrupt shift boundaries, and an unlucky fixed period could strawman the baseline unless the sweep is wide.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Forgetting-prevention machinery is considered necessary because naive continual adaptation degrades, and reset is dismissed as wasteful.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Adaptation state for normalization-level updates is reacquired within tens of batches, so the amortized cost of resets is tiny compared to the compounding cost of drift.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One corruption sequence, one continual method versus entropy minimization with three reset periods, compare time-averaged accuracy in a few GPU-hours.

one_line_idea: Episodic reset-per-shift evaluation protocols overstate test-time adaptation practicality, and realistic recurring mixed-shift streams reverse published method rankings.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Standard protocols evaluate adaptation on one shift at a time, often resetting the model between shifts, while real streams interleave and revisit conditions such as day, night, and weather without announced boundaries.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Method rankings are protocol-dependent, and under unannounced recurring mixed shifts, methods that look strong episodically will underperform simpler or memory-based approaches because their state management assumptions break.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Constructing streams that interleave and revisit shift conditions will produce method rankings with low rank correlation to episodic-protocol rankings, and at least some published methods will fall below the never-adapt baseline. Falsified if: zero (0) published methods fall below the never-adapt baseline on the interleaved, revisiting mixed-shift streams.
why_important: Benchmark protocols function as the field's objective function; if the protocol rewards the wrong behaviors, the literature optimizes for scenarios that do not occur.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Continual adaptation benchmarks exist, but recurring-condition streams with unannounced revisits, explicitly designed to test state reuse, may be an unoccupied evaluation niche.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build recurring mixed streams from existing shift datasets with a hidden condition schedule, evaluate a representative method set, and compare rankings to the episodic protocol on identical underlying data.
main_risk: Stream construction choices such as revisit frequency could themselves determine rankings, so conclusions must be shown stable across schedule randomizations.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Episodic per-shift results are read as predictive of deployment behavior on mixed streams.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Episodic protocols never test whether a method can exploit recurrence or recover from interleaving, which are the dominant structures of real drift.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Interleave two alternating shift conditions into one stream, run three methods, check whether episodic winners still win, one day.

falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A re-evaluation of representative alignment-based methods on foundation-model backbones will show their marginal gain over source-only-plus-self-training shrinking to within noise on the majority of standard adaptation tasks. why_important: If backbone progress dissolved the problem the methods solved, ongoing method development on legacy benchmarks is misallocated effort, and the open problems lie elsewhere.

one_line_idea: Marginal feature-alignment objectives actively hurt adaptation when source and target label distributions differ, and popular benchmarks hide this by having nearly matched label marginals.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Aligning marginal feature distributions across domains is provably harmful when label proportions differ, since forcing marginals together must distort class-conditional structure, yet marginal alignment remains a default component.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Standard benchmark pairs have incidentally similar label marginals, which is why the harm is invisible; introducing controlled label-proportion mismatch will make alignment methods underperform source-only baselines with a severity that grows with the mismatch.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Resampling target label proportions on existing benchmarks to create controlled mismatch will show alignment-based methods degrading below no-adaptation baselines beyond a modest mismatch level, while self-training degrades more gracefully. why_important: Real deployments almost never have matched label proportions across domains, so a failure mode invisible on benchmarks is a failure mode guaranteed in practice.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] The theoretical objection is known, but a quantitative mismatch-severity curve across popular methods on vision benchmarks, framed as a benchmark-design flaw, may be unoccupied territory.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take one benchmark pair, resample target class proportions at several mismatch severities, run marginal-alignment and self-training methods at each severity, and plot adaptation gain versus mismatch.
main_risk: Resampling reduces target sample size at high mismatch, so accuracy changes must be disentangled from sample-size effects with matched-size controls.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Marginal alignment is treated as a safe default that at worst does nothing, and label-proportion mismatch is regarded as a corner case.

one_line_idea: Embedding-space shift detection is dominated by low-level image statistics, masking semantic shifts; band-separated tests are needed to see what actually changed.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Shift detectors operating on deep embeddings report a single shift score, while real changes decompose into low-level factors like compression and color and high-level factors like content and population, with very different operational implications.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Standard embedding statistics respond much more strongly to low-level factors than to semantic factors of equal harm, so a semantic shift co-occurring with a mild low-level change is detected as the low-level change and its semantic component goes unnoticed.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] In factorial scenarios crossing low-level and semantic changes, single-score detectors will show scores dominated by the low-level factor, while a decomposition that separates frequency-band and semantic-subspace components will recover both factors independently. why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Shift attribution into interpretable low-level versus semantic components, validated on factorial scenarios, may be missing from the monitoring literature.

fastest_falsification_experiment: One dataset, apply compression change versus class-mixture change calibrated to equal accuracy harm, compare a standard detector's scores, hours.

problem: [KNOWN FACT] Deployment monitoring is sequential, with decisions made continuously as data arrives, yet most shift-detection research evaluates fixed-sample tests that do not control error under continuous monitoring.

one_line_idea: Shuffling time-stamped datasets hides temporal drift; time-respecting splits materially change both absolute accuracy and model rankings on the same data.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Many vision datasets are collected over months or years and carry timestamps, but standard practice shuffles all data before splitting, destroying temporal structure and hiding any drift between collection and deployment eras.

one_line_idea: The optimal adaptation learning rate under gradual drift is a function of measurable drift speed, and an adaptive-rate law derived from it beats every fixed-rate configuration.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Online adaptation methods use fixed learning rates chosen by benchmark tuning, while drift in deployments varies in speed over time, and rate misconfiguration causes either lag behind the drift or noise amplification.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] There is a stable functional relationship between drift speed, estimable from windowed embedding statistics, and the regret-minimizing adaptation rate, so a controller that sets the rate from estimated speed will approach oracle-rate performance across drift regimes without per-deployment tuning.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across streams spanning slow, fast, and varying drift, the speed-tracking controller will match the best fixed rate in each regime and beat every single fixed rate on the mixed regime, approaching the oracle schedule within a small margin. Falsified if: one or more fixed adaptation rates match or exceed the speed-tracking controller on the mixed-drift regime.
why_important: Rate selection is the main deployment-blocking hyperparameter of online adaptation, and replacing it with a measurement-driven law removes the need for per-site tuning that no operator can perform.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Drift-adaptive step sizes exist in online learning theory; an empirically validated speed-to-rate law for deep vision adaptation with drift-speed estimation from embeddings may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate drift streams with controlled speeds, sweep fixed rates to map the oracle rate per speed, fit the speed-to-rate relationship, then validate the controller on held-out mixed-speed streams.
main_risk: Drift-speed estimation from embeddings may confuse drift with noise bursts, and a controller reacting to noise would amplify exactly what it should damp.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Adaptation rates are treated as method constants to be benchmarked once, rather than as quantities that must track a property of the environment.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Tracking theory in simpler settings makes the optimal rate scale with the drift-to-noise ratio, and there is no reason deep adaptation escapes that structural dependence.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Three drift speeds, five fixed rates, verify the optimal rate shifts with speed and a two-point controller interpolation beats fixed rates on a mixed stream, one day.

one_line_idea: Online adaptation methods are broken by realistic non-uniform arrival processes such as class bursts, and arrival-robustness should be a first-class evaluation axis.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Real input streams arrive with strong temporal structure, bursts of similar content, session effects, and diurnal cycles, while adaptation benchmarks feed methods class-balanced shuffled batches.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Popular adaptation methods implicitly rely on within-window class diversity, so realistic bursty arrival will cause prior-collapse updates and accuracy loss even with zero distribution shift, and method rankings under bursty arrival will differ sharply from shuffled-arrival rankings.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Replaying identical data in shuffled versus bursty orders will produce large accuracy differences for adaptation methods but not for frozen models, with some methods degraded below the frozen baseline purely by arrival order. Falsified if: zero (0) adaptation methods fall below the frozen-model baseline under bursty replay of identical data.
why_important: Arrival structure is universal in deployment and free to simulate in evaluation, so ignoring it inflates reported reliability at no benefit.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Temporally correlated test streams appear in a few papers; arrival-order robustness as a systematic evaluation axis with burst-parameterized stress tests may be unestablished.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fix datasets and shifts, replay streams under parameterized arrival processes varying burst length and class concentration, and measure each method's accuracy as a function of arrival parameters.
main_risk: Bursty replay changes the effective local distribution, so the analysis must separate arrival-order effects from genuine local-distribution effects with frozen-model controls.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Shuffled arrival is treated as a neutral simplification rather than an assumption doing load-bearing work in reported results.

one_line_idea: The synthetic-to-real gap in super-resolution is dominated by unmodeled noise and compression, not by blur-kernel mismatch, so blind-kernel estimation attacks a second-order problem.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Super-resolution models trained on bicubically downsampled pairs degrade sharply on real photographs, and much of the blind-SR literature attributes this gap primarily to unknown blur kernels.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Matching realistic sensor noise and compression statistics alone, while keeping a deliberately wrong bicubic kernel, recovers the majority of the synthetic-to-real transfer gap; kernel realism alone recovers only a minority share.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] In a factorial ablation toggling kernel realism, noise realism, and compression realism independently, the noise and compression factors will show larger main effects on real-photo restoration quality than the kernel factor. Falsified if: training with realistic noise plus compression while keeping the bicubic kernel closes <= 50% of the real-photo restoration quality gap to the fully realistic pipeline (equivalently, kernel realism retains the majority share of the gap in the 2x2x2 factorial).
why_important: Blind-kernel estimation is a large subfield; if kernel mismatch is second-order, research effort and model capacity should be redirected toward noise and compression modeling.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Individual pipelines ablate their own components, but a clean factorial attribution of the synthetic-to-real gap across kernel, noise, and compression with interaction terms may not have been published.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train matched SR models on a 2x2x2 factorial of degradation realism (kernel, noise, compression), evaluate all eight on the same held-out real-photo set, and estimate main effects and interactions of each factor on restoration quality.
main_risk: Real degradations entangle the three factors, so a factorial synthetic design may fail to represent real interaction structure and understate the kernel effect.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Unknown blur kernels are treated as the central obstacle of blind super-resolution, with noise and compression handled as secondary nuisances.

one_line_idea: SR models get amplitude spectra roughly right but phase systematically wrong, and phase error is the better predictor of perceived structural artifacts, motivating phase-aware losses.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Restoration losses operate pointwise or on learned features, without explicit control over how reconstruction error distributes between spectral amplitude and phase, while phase is known to carry structural information in images.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Trained SR models allocate error disproportionately to phase in high frequencies (plausible energy, misplaced structure), phase error correlates with human-perceived structural artifacts better than amplitude error, and adding an explicit phase-coherence term to training reduces structural artifacts at equal amplitude accuracy.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Spectral decomposition of errors across models will show phase-dominated high-frequency error, human artifact ratings will track phase error more than amplitude error, and phase-regularized training will improve artifact ratings. Falsified if: in the spectral decomposition of reconstruction error into amplitude and phase components, the phase component accounts for <= 50% of high-frequency error (does not exceed the amplitude component) across the model panel.
why_important: It offers a physically interpretable account of what perceptual losses vaguely address, and a targeted, cheap loss ingredient.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Spectral analyses of GAN artifacts exist; a phase-centric error accounting and phase-targeted loss for SR may be underexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Decompose reconstruction errors of a model panel into amplitude and phase components per band, collect artifact ratings, correlate, then train matched models with and without phase terms.
main_risk: Global Fourier phase is a crude descriptor for local structure, and windowed analyses add parameter choices that affect conclusions.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Spectral amplitude realism is treated as the main frequency-domain target, with phase left implicit.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Pointwise losses are minimized by hedging phase where uncertain, and adversarial losses enforce marginal statistics that constrain amplitude much more than phase alignment with the source.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Swap the phase of model outputs with ground-truth phase (keeping model amplitude) on a few images; a dramatic perceived-quality jump from ground-truth phase alone demonstrates phase is the binding error.
